topic.title: Web, HTTP, REST & Security
topic.summary: How the web works in an interview: HTTP methods, status codes and caching, REST design, cookies, sessions, JWT and OAuth 2.0 with PKCE, CORS, the OWASP classics (XSS, CSRF, SQL injection), password storage, real-time options and the browser rendering path.
topic.overview:
## What interviewers expect
Every web, backend or full-stack interview includes "how the web works" questions, whatever your framework. For a junior role they usually probe four areas:

1. **HTTP itself** — methods and idempotency, status codes, headers, caching (`Cache-Control`, `ETag`, `304`). You should be able to read a raw request/response and say what each line means.
2. **API design** — REST conventions (nouns, versioning, pagination, error format) and when GraphQL, gRPC, WebSockets or Server-Sent Events fit better.
3. **Auth and browser storage** — cookies vs localStorage, sessions vs JWT, OAuth 2.0 / "Sign in with Google" with PKCE, CORS.
4. **Security basics** — XSS, CSRF, SQL injection (the OWASP Top 10 classics) and how passwords must be stored.

Many service companies and banks/fintechs also ask what happens in the browser after the HTML arrives (the critical rendering path) because it explains performance problems.

## Core ideas that connect everything
- **HTTP is stateless.** Cookies, sessions and tokens exist to add identity on top of it — and each choice moves risk between XSS and CSRF.
- **Status codes, methods and headers are a contract** that browsers, proxies, CDNs and client libraries rely on (retries, caching, redirects). Using them precisely is what separates a good API from a working one.
- **The browser is the security boundary.** The same-origin policy, CORS, SameSite cookies, CSP and HttpOnly are all browser-enforced rules — they protect users, not your server from curl.
- **Never trust input; never store secrets reversibly.** Parameterised queries, output escaping, slow salted password hashes.

## How to study this topic
- Open DevTools → Network on any site and read real requests: methods, status codes, `Cache-Control`, `Set-Cookie`, preflight `OPTIONS` calls.
- Use `curl -i` against your own Express app to see exact headers and status codes.
- Draw the sequence diagrams from this topic from memory: CORS preflight, OAuth code + PKCE, JWT vs session login, cache revalidation.
- For every security question, answer in the same shape: **how the attack works → concrete example → what the attacker gains → layered defences**.

cheatsheet.title: Auth and storage
points: Cookie: ~4 KB, sent automatically; HttpOnly + Secure + SameSite for auth
localStorage: ~5 MB, all tabs, never sent, readable by any script
sessionStorage: one tab, cleared on close
Session = random id + server store (instant revoke); JWT = signed claims (stateless, revoke is hard)
OAuth 2.0 code + PKCE: code_challenge = BASE64URL(SHA256(verifier)); state stops CSRF; OIDC adds id_token

cheatsheet.title: Browser security
points: Origin = scheme + host + port; CORS is browser-enforced opt-in via response headers
Preflight (OPTIONS) for PUT/PATCH/DELETE, JSON bodies, Authorization headers
Credentials: Allow-Credentials true + explicit origin, never *
XSS → escape output, sanitise HTML, CSP, HttpOnly; CSRF → SameSite, CSRF token, Origin check
SQL injection → parameterised queries; passwords → Argon2id/bcrypt/scrypt with per-user salt

cheatsheet.title: Caching
points: max-age = fresh, no request; ETag + If-None-Match → 304 without body
no-cache = store but revalidate; no-store = never store; private = browser only
Hashed assets: public, max-age=31536000, immutable · HTML: no-cache

cheatsheet.title: Real-time and rendering
points: Polling (simple) → long polling → SSE (server→client, auto-reconnect) → WebSocket (full duplex, 101 upgrade)
HTML → DOM, CSS → CSSOM → render tree → layout → paint → composite
CSS is render-blocking; classic scripts block parsing; prefer defer (app) and async (third-party)
Core Web Vitals: LCP ≤ 2.5 s, INP ≤ 200 ms, CLS ≤ 0.1

questions.title: HTTP methods: safe vs idempotent (GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE)
questions.prompt: Explain the main **HTTP methods** and the properties **safe**, **idempotent** and **cacheable**. Why is `PUT` idempotent but `POST` is not? How would you make a payment `POST` safe to retry after a network timeout?
hints: Safe = no state change requested. Idempotent = doing it twice leaves the server in the same state as doing it once.
Idempotency is about server state, not identical responses — DELETE twice can return 204 then 404.
Let the client send a unique Idempotency-Key header; the server stores the result per key and replays it on retries.

approaches.name: Weak answer
approaches.idea: Maps verbs to CRUD only ("POST create, GET read…") and cannot define idempotent, or claims it means "same response every time".

approaches.name: Strong answer
approaches.idea: Defines safe / idempotent / cacheable precisely, places each method, explains why it matters for retries, proxies and caches, distinguishes PUT (replace) from PATCH (partial), and describes the Idempotency-Key pattern for payments.

solution.summary: GET, HEAD and OPTIONS are safe — they only read. PUT and DELETE are idempotent: repeating them leaves the server in the same state as doing them once, so clients and proxies can retry them. POST, and PATCH in general, are not idempotent — retrying a POST can create a duplicate order — so for payments the client sends an Idempotency-Key and the server replays the stored result for a repeated key instead of charging twice.
solution.explanation:
**Definitions (HTTP semantics, RFC 9110)**
- **Safe** — the client does not request any state change; read-only semantics. `GET`, `HEAD`, `OPTIONS`, `TRACE`.
- **Idempotent** — the intended effect of N identical requests equals the effect of one. All safe methods plus **`PUT`** and **`DELETE`**.
- **Cacheable** — responses may be stored and reused: `GET` and `HEAD` (`POST` only with explicit freshness information, which is rare).

**The methods**

| Method | Meaning | Safe | Idempotent | Typical success |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| GET | read a resource | yes | yes | 200 |
| HEAD | GET without a body (size, existence, headers) | yes | yes | 200 |
| OPTIONS | which methods are allowed (CORS preflight) | yes | yes | 204 |
| POST | create a subordinate resource / run a process | no | **no** | 201, 200 or 202 |
| PUT | **replace** the resource at this URL (or create it there) | no | **yes** | 200, 201 or 204 |
| PATCH | **partial** update | no | not guaranteed | 200 or 204 |
| DELETE | remove the resource | no | **yes** | 204 or 200 |

**Why PUT is idempotent and POST is not**
`PUT /users/7 { "name": "Rafi Ahmed", "credits": 50 }` sets the resource to exactly that state — sending it twice leaves the same state. `POST /orders` means "create a *new* order" — twice creates two orders. `PATCH` depends on the body: `{ "name": "Rafi" }` (set a field) is idempotent; a custom increment operation such as `{ "op": "increment", "path": "/credits", "value": 10 }` is not, and neither is a JSON Patch `add` to `/items/-` (it appends every time).
`DELETE` twice: the first returns 204, the second 404 — different responses, **same server state**, so it is still idempotent. Idempotency is about the effect on the server, not about identical responses.

**Why it matters**
- Networks fail *after* the server did the work (the response is lost). HTTP clients, proxies and service meshes may automatically retry idempotent requests; they must not blindly retry a POST.
- Browsers warn before re-submitting a POST form; in practice caches only store GET/HEAD responses.
- Never change state on GET (`GET /orders/42/delete`): crawlers, link previews and browser prefetching will trigger it.

**Making POST safe to retry: idempotency keys**
1. The client generates a unique key (a UUID) per logical operation and sends `Idempotency-Key: 9f1c…` with `POST /payments`.
2. The server processes the request once and stores `key → response` (Redis or a DB table with a unique index, TTL ~24 h).
3. A retry with the same key gets the **stored response** — no second charge. A duplicate that arrives while the first is still running gets `409 Conflict` (use an atomic "insert if absent", e.g. Redis `SET NX`, to detect it).

Stripe's API and many payment gateways use exactly this pattern.
keyPoints: Safe: GET, HEAD, OPTIONS (read-only). Idempotent: safe methods + PUT and DELETE
POST is not idempotent; PATCH is not guaranteed to be
Idempotency is about server state, not identical responses
Clients and proxies may retry idempotent requests automatically
Idempotency-Key header makes POST /payments retry-safe

visuals.caption: A small in-memory server following HTTP semantics; ids shortened (the snippet uses UUIDs).

steps.note: Starting state: one user and no payments. Watch which requests change the state when they are **repeated**.
PUT **replaces** user 7 with exactly this body.
The client retries the same PUT after a timeout: the state is **identical** to after one call → idempotent, safe to retry.
A naive payment endpoint without keys: POST creates payment p1 and charges 500.
The response was lost, so the app retries the POST → a **second charge** (p2). POST is not idempotent.
The snippet's endpoint: the client sends `Idempotency-Key: k-77`. First time → charge once (p3) and store the response under k-77.
Retry with the **same key** → the stored 201 response is replayed. No new row, no second charge.
A PATCH with a custom *increment* operation: credits 50 → 60.
Retrying it gives 70 — this PATCH is **not** idempotent. (A PATCH that sets `credits: 60` would be.)
DELETE removes user 7 → 204.
Second DELETE → 404, a different response but the **same server state**: DELETE is idempotent.

followUps.question: PUT vs PATCH?
followUps.answer: PUT sends the complete new representation and replaces the resource (missing fields are cleared); PATCH sends only the changes (JSON Merge Patch or JSON Patch). PUT is idempotent by definition; PATCH only if the patch itself is (set vs increment).

followUps.question: How do you handle two simultaneous requests with the same idempotency key?
followUps.answer: Reserve the key atomically before doing the work (Redis SET key NX, or an insert with a unique index). The second request sees the reservation and gets 409 Conflict (or waits); once the first finishes, later retries get the stored response. Also store a hash of the request body with the key: the same key with a different body is a client bug, so reject it (422) instead of replaying.

questions.title: HTTP status codes you must know (and the commonly confused pairs)
questions.prompt: What do the five classes of **HTTP status codes** mean? Which codes should an API return for: a created resource, a successful delete, invalid input, a missing login, a logged-in user without permission, a duplicate email, too many requests, and a crashed upstream service? Explain **401 vs 403** and **301 vs 302 vs 307 vs 308**.
hints: First digit: 1 informational, 2 success, 3 redirect, 4 the client's fault, 5 the server's fault.
401 means 'I don't know who you are'; 403 means 'I know who you are, and the answer is no'.
307/308 guarantee the method and body are kept on redirect; 301/302 historically let browsers switch POST to GET.

approaches.name: Weak answer
approaches.idea: "200 OK, 404 not found, 500 error" — and returning 200 with { success: false } for failures.

approaches.name: Strong answer
approaches.idea: Explains the classes, picks a precise code for each scenario with its companion header (Location, Retry-After, WWW-Authenticate, Allow), and resolves the confusing pairs: 401/403, 400/422, 404/410, 301/302/307/308, 502/503/504.

solution.summary: 2xx means success, 3xx redirect, 4xx the client did something wrong, 5xx the server failed. For an API: 201 + Location on create, 204 on delete, 400 (or 422) for invalid input, 401 when not authenticated, 403 when authenticated but not allowed, 404 not found, 409 for a duplicate or conflict, 429 with Retry-After for rate limiting, 500 for a bug, and 502/503/504 when an upstream or the service itself is unavailable.
solution.explanation:
**The five classes**
- **1xx informational** — `101 Switching Protocols` (WebSocket upgrade), `103 Early Hints`.
- **2xx success** — `200 OK`, `201 Created` (+ `Location`), `202 Accepted` (queued for asynchronous processing), `204 No Content` (success, no body).
- **3xx redirection** — `301`/`308` permanent, `302`/`307` temporary, `303 See Other`, `304 Not Modified` (cache revalidation).
- **4xx client error** — the request is wrong; sending it again unchanged won't help (exceptions: `408` and `429` mean "try again later").
- **5xx server error** — the server failed; retrying later might help.

**The ones interviewers probe**
- `400 Bad Request` — malformed JSON, wrong types. `422 Unprocessable Content` — well-formed but fails validation rules. Many APIs use 400 for both; just be consistent.
- `401 Unauthorized` — despite the name it means **unauthenticated**: missing, invalid or expired credentials. Per RFC 9110 it must carry a `WWW-Authenticate` header (e.g. `Bearer`). The fix is to log in.
- `403 Forbidden` — **authenticated but not allowed** (a normal user calling an admin endpoint). Logging in again won't help.
- `404 Not Found` — no such resource; also used instead of 403 so you don't reveal that a private resource exists. `410 Gone` — it existed and was removed permanently.
- `405 Method Not Allowed` (+ `Allow`), `409 Conflict` (duplicate email, edit conflict), `413 Content Too Large`, `415 Unsupported Media Type`, `429 Too Many Requests` (+ `Retry-After`).
- `500 Internal Server Error` — an unhandled bug. `502 Bad Gateway` — a proxy/gateway got an invalid response from the upstream. `503 Service Unavailable` — overloaded or in maintenance (+ `Retry-After`). `504 Gateway Timeout` — the upstream didn't answer in time.

**Redirects**

| Code | Permanent? | Method when the client follows it |
|---|---|---|
| 301 Moved Permanently | yes | may change POST to GET (historical browser behaviour) |
| 302 Found | no | may change POST to GET |
| 303 See Other | no | always GET (redirect after a form POST) |
| 307 Temporary Redirect | no | **same method and body** |
| 308 Permanent Redirect | yes | **same method and body** |

**Rule of thumb**: never return `200` with `{ "success": false }`. Monitoring, caches, retries and client libraries all branch on the status code.
keyPoints: 2xx success, 3xx redirect, 4xx client error, 5xx server error
201 + Location on create; 204 for success without a body
401 = not authenticated; 403 = authenticated but not allowed
409 for conflicts, 429 + Retry-After for rate limits
502 bad upstream response, 503 overloaded/maintenance, 504 upstream timeout

followUps.question: A user requests another user's private document. 403 or 404?
followUps.answer: 404 is often better: 403 confirms the document exists, which can leak information (e.g. that an account or file id is valid). Use 403 when the resource's existence isn't secret, such as an admin-only page.

followUps.question: What status for a long-running export job?
followUps.answer: 202 Accepted with a Location header pointing to a status resource (/jobs/123). The client polls it (or gets a webhook/SSE event); when done, the status resource links to the result.

questions.title: REST API design best practices (naming, versioning, pagination, errors)
questions.prompt: You're designing the public REST API of an e-commerce app (products, orders, users). Explain your conventions for **resource naming**, **filtering and sorting**, **versioning**, **pagination** and the **error format** — including the trade-off between offset and cursor pagination.
hints: URLs name things (nouns); HTTP methods are the verbs.
What goes wrong with ?page=2 when new items are inserted while a user is scrolling?
A cursor remembers the last item seen (its sort key) and asks for items after it; errors should share one machine-readable shape.

approaches.name: Weak answer
approaches.idea: Verb URLs like /getAllProducts, ?page= on every list with no limit cap, and ad-hoc error strings with status 200.

approaches.name: Strong answer
approaches.idea: Plural nouns and shallow nesting, query parameters for filter/sort/fields with allowlists, /v1 versioning with additive changes, cursor pagination for feeds and offset for small admin tables, RFC 9457 problem details, plus idempotency keys, rate-limit headers and an OpenAPI contract.

solution.summary: Model the API as resources: plural nouns like /v1/products and /v1/users/42/orders, HTTP methods as the verbs, and query parameters for filtering, sorting and field selection. Version in the URL (/v1) and make only additive changes within a version. Paginate every list — offset for small admin tables where users jump to page N, cursor (keyset) for large or fast-changing feeds — and return every error in one consistent JSON shape with a machine-readable code.
solution.explanation:
**Naming**
- Nouns, plural, lowercase, hyphenated: `/v1/products`, `/v1/products/42`, `/v1/users/42/orders`, `/v1/order-items`.
- The HTTP method is the verb: `POST /v1/orders`, not `POST /v1/createOrder`. For actions that aren't CRUD, model a sub-resource (`POST /v1/orders/42/cancellation`) or use the pragmatic `POST /v1/orders/42/cancel`.
- Nest at most one or two levels; deeper relations become filters: `/v1/orders?userId=42&status=paid`.

**Filtering, sorting, fields**
`GET /v1/products?category=keyboards&minPrice=20&sort=-createdAt,price&fields=id,name,price&limit=20`. Allowlist the sortable and filterable fields — never pass them straight into a database query.

**Versioning**
- **URI** (`/v1/...`) is the most common: visible, easy to route, cache and test. Header-based (`Accept: application/vnd.shop.v2+json`) keeps URLs clean but is harder to use.
- Additive, non-breaking changes (a new optional field, a new endpoint) stay in v1. Breaking changes (renaming/removing fields, changing types or meaning) → v2; run both and announce the end of v1 (`Deprecation` / `Sunset` headers, changelog, emails).

**Pagination**
- **Offset/limit** (`?page=3&limit=20` → skip 40): simple, supports "jump to page 7" and total counts. But the database still walks every skipped row (slow at page 10,000), and inserts or deletes between requests cause **duplicates or missed items** (see the visual).
- **Cursor/keyset** (`?limit=20&after=WzE3Njk…`): the cursor encodes the last item's sort key (e.g. `createdAt` plus `id` as a tie-breaker). The next query is `WHERE (created_at, id) < (:c, :id) ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 20` — index-friendly, constant speed, stable under inserts, but no random page jumps. Infinite-scroll feeds and Stripe-style list APIs work this way.
- Always cap `limit` (e.g. max 100) and return `nextCursor`/`hasMore` (or `total` for offset).

**Errors** — one shape everywhere, e.g. **RFC 9457 Problem Details** (`Content-Type: application/problem+json`): `type`, `title`, `status`, `detail`, `instance`, plus your own `code` and field-level `errors`. Correct status codes; never 200 for failures; no stack traces.

**Also mention**: consistent camelCase JSON, ISO-8601 UTC timestamps, `201 + Location`, idempotency keys for payments, rate-limit headers, ETags for caching, authentication via cookie or `Authorization` header, and an **OpenAPI** document as the contract.
keyPoints: Plural nouns, HTTP verbs, shallow nesting, query params for filter/sort/fields
Version in the URL (/v1); only additive changes within a version
Offset pagination breaks under inserts and is slow when deep; cursor/keyset is stable and index-friendly
Always cap limit and return nextCursor / hasMore
One error format (problem details) with a machine-readable code and correct status

visuals.title: Offset vs cursor pagination when a new post arrives
visuals.caption: Pages computed with the listPage function from the solution and a plain OFFSET slice.

steps.note: Offset pagination, page 1: `ORDER BY createdAt DESC LIMIT 3 OFFSET 0` → posts 7, 6, 5.
While the user reads page 1, a new post (id 8) is published. It lands at the **top** of the feed and pushes every other post down one position.
Page 2: `OFFSET 3` now starts at the old post 5 → the user sees **post 5 twice**. (A delete would make them miss a post instead.) Deep offsets are also slow: the DB walks every skipped row.
Cursor pagination, page 1: same posts 7, 6, 5, plus `nextCursor` — the base64url of the last item's sort key `[580, 5]` (createdAt 09:40 stored as minutes since midnight, id 5).
Post 8 arrives, then page 2 asks for items **strictly after** (09:40, id 5). The new post does not shift anything: 4, 3, 2 — no duplicate, and the query uses an index on (createdAt, id).

rows: 400 application/problem+json with code and field errors

pitfalls: Verbs in URLs and GET requests that change state
Unbounded list endpoints with no maximum limit
Deep OFFSET pagination on large, fast-changing tables
Breaking changes shipped without a new version

followUps.question: How would you design filtering so it is safe?
followUps.answer: Accept only allowlisted fields and operators (status, minPrice, sort among createdAt/price), validate types with a schema, map them to parameterised queries, and back common combinations with indexes; reject anything else with 400.

followUps.question: When is offset pagination still the right choice?
followUps.answer: Small or slowly changing datasets where users need page numbers and totals — admin tables, search results with "page 3 of 12". Cap the maximum page depth to avoid expensive deep offsets.

questions.title: Cookies vs localStorage vs sessionStorage
questions.prompt: Compare **cookies**, **localStorage** and **sessionStorage**: capacity, lifetime, scope, whether they are sent to the server, and who can read them. Where would you store an auth token, a theme preference and a half-filled checkout form?
hints: Only one of the three travels to the server automatically with every request.
sessionStorage is scoped to one tab; localStorage to the whole origin; cookies to a domain and path.
Any JavaScript on the page — including injected XSS — can read localStorage, but not an HttpOnly cookie.

approaches.name: Weak answer
approaches.idea: "Cookies are old and small, localStorage is bigger, so put the JWT in localStorage."

approaches.name: Strong answer
approaches.idea: Compares size, lifetime, scope, server visibility and JavaScript access; explains HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite, Max-Age, Domain and Path; picks storage per use case with the XSS/CSRF trade-off; mentions IndexedDB for larger data.

solution.summary: Cookies are small (about 4 KB each), set by the server or by JavaScript, and sent automatically with every matching request — with HttpOnly they are invisible to JavaScript, which makes them the right place for session ids and auth tokens. localStorage (about 5 MB per origin) persists until cleared and is shared by every tab of the origin; sessionStorage has the same API but lives only as long as one tab. Neither storage API is ever sent to the server, and any script on the page can read them, so they are for non-sensitive UI state.
solution.explanation:
**Cookies**
- Set by the server with a `Set-Cookie` response header (or by JS through `document.cookie` unless HttpOnly). About **4 KB** per cookie.
- **Sent automatically** with every request to a matching domain and path → the server can read them, but they add bytes to every request.
- Attributes:
  - `Expires` / `Max-Age` — without them it is a **session cookie**, deleted when the browser session ends.
  - `Domain`, `Path` — scope.
  - **`Secure`** — only sent over HTTPS.
  - **`HttpOnly`** — not readable by JavaScript (`document.cookie` won't show it).
  - **`SameSite`** — `Strict` (never sent on cross-site requests), `Lax` (sent on cross-site top-level GET navigations such as clicking a link, but not on cross-site POSTs, fetch calls, iframes or images; Chrome and Edge apply it when SameSite is missing), `None` (always sent; requires `Secure`).
- Best for: **session ids and auth tokens** (HttpOnly + Secure + SameSite), server-rendered preferences such as language.

**localStorage**
- About **5 MB** per origin (browser-dependent), strings only (`JSON.stringify` objects), **synchronous** API that runs on the main thread.
- Persists **until explicitly cleared**; shared by **all tabs and windows of the same origin**; a `storage` event notifies *other* tabs of changes.
- **Never sent to the server**, and readable by **any** script on the origin → an XSS bug can read everything in it.
- Best for: theme, language, dismissed banners, cached non-sensitive data.

**sessionStorage**
- Same API and size class, but scoped to **one tab** (top-level browsing context) and origin. Survives reloads, cleared when the tab closes. A new tab starts empty (duplicating a tab copies it).
- Best for: per-tab state such as a multi-step checkout draft, so two open tabs don't overwrite each other.

**Bigger or structured data** → **IndexedDB** (asynchronous, much larger quotas, used by offline apps/PWAs).

**Where to put what**
- Auth token or session id → **HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite=Lax cookie** (and CSRF protection for state-changing requests).
- Theme preference → **localStorage** (or a normal cookie if the server must render the theme without a flash).
- Half-filled checkout form → **sessionStorage**.
- Never store passwords, card numbers or long-lived tokens in localStorage.

questions.title: Session-based vs JWT (token-based) authentication
questions.prompt: Compare **server-side sessions** with **JWT** (stateless token) authentication. How does each identify the user on a request, how do they scale across several servers, and how do you log a user out or revoke access? When would you choose each?
hints: Where does the user's login state live — on the server, or inside the token the client holds?
Revocation: deleting a server-side session is instant. What can you delete when the token itself is the proof?
Stateless verification helps distributed systems; instant revocation helps security. Short-lived access tokens + refresh tokens combine both.

approaches.name: Weak answer
approaches.idea: "JWT is modern and more secure; sessions are old." Neither is inherently more secure — it is a trade-off.

approaches.name: Strong answer
approaches.idea: Explains both mechanisms (opaque id + store lookup vs signed self-contained claims), compares scaling, revocation, size, staleness and cross-service use, separates "session vs JWT" from "cookie vs header", and recommends sessions for classic web apps and short-lived JWT + refresh tokens for multi-client APIs.

solution.summary: With sessions the server keeps the login state in a store (Redis or a database) and gives the browser only a random session id in an HttpOnly cookie; every request looks that id up, and logout simply deletes it. With JWTs the server signs the user's claims into the token itself, so any server can verify a request without a lookup — easy to scale across services — but a token stays valid until it expires, so you pair short-lived access tokens with revocable refresh tokens.
solution.explanation:
**Session-based (stateful)**
1. Login → the server creates `sessions[sid] = { userId: 42, role: 'user', expires }` in Redis or the database.
2. It responds `Set-Cookie: sid=<random 256-bit id>; HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax`.
3. Every request: the cookie arrives → look up `sid` → `req.user`.
4. Logout, ban or password change → **delete the session**: access ends immediately.
- Scaling: all instances must share the store (Redis), or you need sticky sessions.
- The cookie is tiny and opaque; the session can hold any server-side data.

**JWT-based (stateless)**
1. Login → the server signs `{ sub: 42, role: 'user', exp }` with its key.
2. The client keeps the token (HttpOnly cookie, or memory + `Authorization: Bearer`).
3. Every request: verify signature and `exp` — **no lookup** — and build `req.user` from the claims.
4. "Logout" = the client discards the token, but **a copied token stays valid until `exp`**.
- Scaling: any server or microservice holding the key (or the public key for RS256) can verify → great for distributed systems, mobile apps and third-party APIs.
- Bigger (hundreds of bytes per request), and claims go stale (a demoted admin's old token still says `admin` until it expires).
- Fixes: short access-token lifetime (5–15 min) + a refresh token stored server-side and **rotated** (so it can be revoked), or a deny-list of token ids (`jti`) — which brings back state.

**Common misconceptions**
- "JWT is more secure" — no. Security depends on where the token is stored (HttpOnly cookie vs localStorage), how long it lives and whether it can be revoked.
- "Sessions don't scale" — a Redis lookup takes well under a millisecond; most apps never outgrow it.
- Both can travel in cookies; "cookie or header" is a separate decision from "session or JWT".

**Choosing**
- A web app on one site (admin panel, internet banking) → **sessions**: simple and instantly revocable.
- Many clients and services (mobile apps, SPA + microservices, partner APIs) → **short-lived JWT access tokens + refresh tokens**, often issued by an identity provider (Keycloak, Auth0, Cognito) via OAuth 2.0 / OpenID Connect.
keyPoints: Session: random id in an HttpOnly cookie, state in Redis/DB, one lookup per request
JWT: signed claims verified without a lookup — scales across services
Sessions revoke instantly; JWTs live until exp → short access tokens + refresh-token rotation
Both can be carried in cookies; storage choice is a separate decision
Sessions for single-site web apps; JWT/OAuth for mobile, SPAs + microservices, partner APIs

followUps.question: How does refresh-token rotation work?
followUps.answer: Each refresh request returns a new access token and a new refresh token, and invalidates the old refresh token. If an old (already used) refresh token shows up again, it was stolen — revoke the whole token family and force a new login.

followUps.question: Can you make sessions stateless too?
followUps.answer: Partly: signed/encrypted cookie sessions (e.g. iron-session) keep data in the cookie like a JWT and share its revocation problem. Most teams keep server-side sessions in Redis because instant revocation is the point.

questions.title: What is CORS? (same-origin policy and preflight requests)
questions.prompt: Your React app on `http://localhost:3000` calls your Express API on `http://localhost:4000` and the console says *blocked by CORS policy*. Explain the **same-origin policy**, what **CORS** is, when the browser sends a **preflight** `OPTIONS` request, how cookies (credentials) change the rules, and how to fix the error properly.
hints: An origin is scheme + host + port. Are localhost:3000 and localhost:4000 the same origin?
CORS is enforced by the browser using response headers from the server. curl and Postman do not care.
A JSON body, PUT/PATCH/DELETE, or an Authorization header makes a request non-simple, so the browser asks permission with OPTIONS first.

approaches.name: Weak answer
approaches.idea: "CORS is a server security feature; fix it with Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *." Wrong on both counts.

approaches.name: Strong answer
approaches.idea: Explains the same-origin policy, CORS as a browser-enforced opt-in, simple vs preflighted requests with the exact headers, the credentials rules (no * with credentials, Vary: Origin), and the correct fixes: an allowlist in cors() or serving both through one origin via a proxy.

solution.summary: Browsers enforce the same-origin policy: a page may send requests to another origin, but its JavaScript cannot read the response unless that server opts in with CORS headers such as Access-Control-Allow-Origin. For non-simple requests — JSON bodies, PUT/PATCH/DELETE, an Authorization header — the browser first sends an OPTIONS preflight and only sends the real request if the server approves. CORS is enforced by the browser, not the server, so the fix is to allowlist the frontend origin on the API (or serve both through one origin), never to switch security off.
solution.explanation:
**Origin** = scheme + host + port. `http://localhost:3000` and `http://localhost:4000` are **different origins**; so are `http://` vs `https://`, and `app.example.com` vs `api.example.com`.

**Same-origin policy (SOP)** — JavaScript from origin A may *send* many kinds of requests to origin B, but cannot *read* B's responses (or B's cookies and DOM). Without it, any website you visit could call your bank's API with your cookies and read the results.

**CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing)** — a way for server B to tell the browser "origin A may read my responses", through response headers. The **browser** enforces it; servers, curl and Postman ignore it. CORS is **not** authentication and does not protect your API from non-browser clients.

**Simple requests** — `GET`, `HEAD`, or `POST` with only CORS-safelisted headers and a `Content-Type` of `text/plain`, `multipart/form-data` or `application/x-www-form-urlencoded`. The browser sends them directly with an `Origin` header. If the response lacks a matching `Access-Control-Allow-Origin`, the browser hides the response from JavaScript — but the server **already processed** the request.

**Preflighted requests** — everything else: `PUT`, `PATCH`, `DELETE`, `Content-Type: application/json`, `Authorization` or custom headers.
1. The browser sends `OPTIONS /api/tasks/7` with `Origin`, `Access-Control-Request-Method: PUT` and `Access-Control-Request-Headers: content-type`.
2. The server answers `204` with `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: http://localhost:3000`, `Access-Control-Allow-Methods`, `Access-Control-Allow-Headers` and optionally `Access-Control-Max-Age: 600` (cache the preflight).
3. Only then does the browser send the real `PUT`; its response also needs `Access-Control-Allow-Origin`.

**Credentials (cookies)**
- The client must opt in: `fetch(url, { credentials: 'include' })`.
- The server must send `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true` **and** a specific origin — `*` is not allowed with credentials — plus `Vary: Origin` so caches don't mix responses for different origins.
- The cookies themselves still obey their `SameSite` rules.

**Fixing "blocked by CORS policy" correctly**
- Configure the API with an allowlist: `app.use(cors({ origin: ['http://localhost:3000', 'https://app.example.com'], credentials: true }))`.
- Or avoid cross-origin calls entirely: serve frontend and API from one origin through a reverse proxy (Nginx) or framework rewrites (Next.js `rewrites` from `/api/*` to Express) — no preflights and simpler cookies.
- Don't: reflect any `Origin` with credentials, install "disable CORS" browser extensions, or use `mode: 'no-cors'` (you get an opaque response you can't read).
keyPoints: Origin = scheme + host + port; SOP stops JS reading cross-origin responses
CORS response headers let the server opt in; the browser enforces them
Non-simple requests (JSON, PUT/DELETE, Authorization) trigger an OPTIONS preflight
Credentials need Allow-Credentials: true and an explicit origin (never *)
CORS doesn't protect the API from curl — use auth; or avoid CORS with a same-origin proxy

followUps.question: How does a Next.js rewrite avoid CORS?
followUps.answer: The browser calls /api/... on its own origin; the Next.js server proxies it to Express server-to-server. The browser never makes a cross-origin request, so there are no preflights and cookies stay first-party.

questions.title: OAuth 2.0 Authorization Code flow with PKCE ('Sign in with Google')
questions.prompt: Explain how **"Sign in with Google"** works using the **OAuth 2.0 Authorization Code flow with PKCE**. Name the roles, walk through each redirect and request, and explain what **PKCE** and the **state** parameter protect against. How is **OpenID Connect** related?
hints: Four roles: the user, your app (client), the authorization server and the resource server (API).
The browser only ever carries a short-lived authorization code; tokens are fetched by a separate back-channel request.
PKCE: the app keeps a random code_verifier secret and sends only its SHA-256 hash (code_challenge) up front; the token request must present the verifier, so a stolen code is useless.

approaches.name: Weak answer
approaches.idea: "OAuth is a login protocol: Google sends my app the user's token in the URL." Confuses authorization with authentication and describes the deprecated implicit flow.

approaches.name: Strong answer
approaches.idea: Separates OAuth (delegated authorization) from OIDC (authentication via id_token), walks through redirect → consent → code → back-channel token exchange, explains state (CSRF), PKCE (code interception) and why the implicit flow is deprecated, and covers how tokens are used and refreshed.

solution.summary: OAuth 2.0 lets a user grant an app limited access to their data without sharing their password. In the Authorization Code flow with PKCE the app redirects the user to the authorization server with a code_challenge (the SHA-256 hash of a secret code_verifier) and a random state; after login and consent the app receives a short-lived code, then exchanges code + code_verifier for tokens over a direct back-channel request. PKCE makes an intercepted code useless, state prevents CSRF, and OpenID Connect adds an id_token so the same flow can be used for "Sign in with Google".
solution.explanation:
**Roles**
- **Resource owner** — the user.
- **Client** — your app (server-side web app, SPA or mobile app).
- **Authorization server** — authenticates the user and issues tokens (Google, GitHub, Keycloak, Auth0).
- **Resource server** — the API that accepts access tokens (Google Calendar API, your own API).

**The flow**
1. **Prepare**: the app creates a random `code_verifier` (43–128 characters), computes `code_challenge = BASE64URL(SHA256(code_verifier))`, and a random `state` (plus a `nonce` for OpenID Connect). It keeps the verifier and state in the user's session.
2. **Redirect** the browser to the authorize endpoint: `response_type=code`, `client_id`, `redirect_uri`, `scope=openid email profile`, `state`, `code_challenge`, `code_challenge_method=S256`.
3. The user **logs in and consents** on the provider's page — your app never sees the password.
4. The provider **redirects back** to `https://app.example.com/callback?code=…&state=…`. The app checks that `state` equals the stored value (**CSRF protection**: an attacker can't inject their own code into your session).
5. **Token exchange** over the back channel (server-to-server or a direct `fetch`, not via the address bar): `POST /token` with `grant_type=authorization_code`, `code`, `redirect_uri`, `client_id`, **`code_verifier`** (and `client_secret` for confidential server-side clients).
6. The authorization server hashes the verifier, compares it with the challenge it stored in step 2, and returns an **access token** (short-lived), optionally a **refresh token**, and with OpenID Connect an **id_token** (a signed JWT describing the user: `sub`, `email`, `name`).
7. The app calls APIs with `Authorization: Bearer <access token>` and uses the refresh token to get new access tokens.

**Why PKCE (Proof Key for Code Exchange)?**
A public client (SPA, mobile app) cannot keep a `client_secret`. If an attacker intercepts the authorization code — a malicious app registered for the same custom URL scheme, a leaked log, a Referer header — they could exchange it for tokens. With PKCE they also need the `code_verifier`, which never left the legitimate app; only its hash travelled. The OAuth 2.0 Security Best Current Practice (RFC 9700) requires PKCE for public clients and recommends it for confidential ones, and the OAuth 2.1 draft requires it for all clients; the old **implicit flow** (tokens straight in the URL fragment) is deprecated.

**OAuth vs OpenID Connect**
OAuth 2.0 is about **authorization** — delegated access ("this app may read your calendar"). **OpenID Connect (OIDC)** is a layer on top for **authentication**: requesting the `openid` scope returns an `id_token` that tells the app *who the user is*. "Sign in with Google" is OIDC using the authorization code flow with PKCE.

Other grant types: **client credentials** (service-to-service, no user), **device authorization** (smart TVs, CLIs), and the **refresh token** grant.

code.code:
import base64
import hashlib
import secrets


def create_pkce_pair():
    code_verifier = secrets.token_urlsafe(32)  # 43 chars, base64url without padding
    digest = hashlib.sha256(code_verifier.encode("ascii")).digest()
    code_challenge = base64.urlsafe_b64encode(digest).rstrip(b"=").decode("ascii")
    return code_verifier, code_challenge


def verify_pkce(code_verifier, stored_challenge):
    digest = hashlib.sha256(code_verifier.encode("ascii")).digest()
    computed = base64.urlsafe_b64encode(digest).rstrip(b"=").decode("ascii")
    return secrets.compare_digest(computed, stored_challenge)  # constant-time


# RFC 7636 test vector
print(verify_pkce("dBjftJeZ4CVP-mB92K27uhbUJU1p1r_wW1gFWFOEjXk",
                  "E9Melhoa2OwvFrEMTJguCHaoeK1t8URWbuGJSstw-cM"))  # True

followUps.question: What is in an id_token and how do you validate it?

questions.title: XSS, CSRF and SQL injection: how they work and how to prevent them
questions.prompt: Explain **Cross-Site Scripting (XSS)**, **Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF)** and **SQL injection**: how each attack works with a concrete example, what the attacker gains, and which defences you would implement. How do they relate to the **OWASP Top 10**?
hints: XSS: whose browser runs the attacker's script, and with which site's privileges?
CSRF: the browser attaches cookies automatically, even when another site triggers the request.
SQL injection: what happens when user input is concatenated into the SQL string instead of being sent as a parameter?

approaches.name: Weak answer
approaches.idea: One-line definitions and "sanitize the input" as the answer to everything.

approaches.name: Strong answer
approaches.idea: For each attack: mechanism + concrete payload + impact + layered defences (XSS: contextual output encoding, safe templating, HTML sanitising, CSP, HttpOnly. CSRF: SameSite, CSRF tokens, Origin checks, no state change on GET. SQLi: parameterised queries, allowlisted identifiers, least privilege), mapped to OWASP categories.

solution.summary: XSS is when attacker-supplied script runs in another user's browser inside your site, so it can act as that user — prevented by escaping output for its context, sanitising any HTML you allow, a Content-Security-Policy and HttpOnly cookies. CSRF tricks a logged-in user's browser into sending a state-changing request with their cookies — prevented by SameSite cookies, CSRF tokens and Origin checks. SQL injection happens when input is concatenated into a query — prevented by parameterised queries. Injection (which includes XSS) and broken access control (which includes CSRF) are core OWASP Top 10 categories.
solution.explanation: **OWASP Top 10** — the Open Worldwide Application Security Project's list of the most critical web application risks. In the current **2025** edition **A01 Broken Access Control** (which includes CSRF) is still #1, and **A05 Injection** (A03 in the 2021 edition) covers SQL, NoSQL and OS-command injection **and XSS**. **1. Cross-Site Scripting (XSS)** The attacker gets **their JavaScript to run in a victim's browser on your origin**. - **Stored**: a product review containing `` is saved and rendered for every visitor. - **Reflected**: `/search?q=` is echoed into the page; the victim clicks a crafted link. - **DOM-based**: client code does `el.innerHTML = location.hash.slice(1)`. Impact: read non-HttpOnly cookies and everything in localStorage, perform actions as the user, show fake login forms, log keystrokes. Defences: - **Escape output for its context** (HTML text, attribute, URL, JavaScript). React, Vue and Angular escape `{text}` by default — avoid `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` / `v-html`, `innerHTML` and `eval` with untrusted data. - If you must accept HTML (rich-text editor), **sanitise** it with an allowlist library (DOMPurify). - **Content-Security-Policy**, e.g. `script-src 'self'` or nonces, so injected inline scripts don't run. - **HttpOnly** cookies so the session token can't be read. **2. Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF)** The victim is logged in to `bank.example` (session cookie). They visit `evil.example`, which auto-submits a hidden form: `POST https://bank.example/transfer` with `to=attacker&amount=50000`. If the cookie is sent on cross-site requests, the bank receives a perfectly authenticated request. The attacker can't read the response — they only need the side effect. Defences: - **SameSite=Lax or Strict** cookies — not sent on cross-site POSTs (Chromium-based browsers default to Lax, but always set it explicitly). SameSite is about the *site*, so a request from a compromised subdomain still counts as same-site — keep tokens or Origin checks for sensitive actions. - **CSRF tokens** — a random per-session value in a hidden field or header that evil.example cannot read (synchronizer token or signed double-submit cookie). - Check the **`Origin`** (or `Sec-Fetch-Site`) header on state-changing requests. - Never change state with GET; re-authenticate for critical actions. - An API authenticated only by an `Authorization: Bearer` header is not CSRF-able (the browser never adds it) — but that token is then exposed to XSS. **3. SQL injection** ``` SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = '' input: ' OR 1=1 -- result: SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = '' OR 1=1 --' ``` `OR 1=1` matches every row and `--` comments out the rest, so a login query returns the first user (often the admin). `UNION SELECT` payloads read other tables; stacked queries can modify data. Defences: - **Parameterised queries / prepared statements**: `WHERE email = ?` with the value sent separately — input is always data, never SQL. ORMs (Hibernate/JPA, Prisma, Sequelize) do this unless you build raw SQL strings yourself. - Identifiers (an `ORDER BY` column) can't be parameters → **allowlist** them. - A least-privilege database account (the app user can't `DROP TABLE`), and no raw database errors shown to users. - The NoSQL version: `{ "password": { "$ne": null } }` → validate types and use Mongoose `sanitizeFilter`. **One-line contrast** — XSS abuses the user's trust in your site (attacker code runs in *their* browser); CSRF abuses your site's trust in the user's browser (cookies sent automatically); SQL injection abuses your server's trust in input (data becomes code in *your* database).

code.code:
import sqlite3

db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.executescript("""
CREATE TABLE users (id INTEGER, email TEXT, role TEXT);
INSERT INTO users VALUES (1, 'admin@shop.example', 'admin'), (2, 'mitu@shop.example', 'user');
""")

email = "' OR 1=1 --"

# VULNERABLE: the input becomes part of the SQL text
unsafe = db.execute(f"SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = '{email}'").fetchall()

# SAFE: the driver sends the value separately; it can never change the query's structure
safe = db.execute("SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = ?", (email,)).fetchall()

print(len(unsafe), len(safe))  # 2 0

keyPoints: XSS = attacker script runs in the victim’s browser on your origin → escape output, sanitise HTML, CSP, HttpOnly
CSRF = victim’s browser sends an authenticated request it didn’t intend → SameSite cookies, CSRF tokens, Origin checks
SQL injection = input becomes SQL → parameterised queries, allowlisted identifiers, least-privilege DB user
OWASP Top 10 (2025): A01 Broken Access Control (incl. CSRF), A05 Injection (incl. XSS; A03 in 2021)
Defence in depth: validation is not a substitute for escaping or parameterisation

followUps.question: What does a Content-Security-Policy actually do against XSS?
followUps.answer: It tells the browser which sources may provide scripts, styles, images and frames. With script-src 'self' (or nonces/hashes) and no 'unsafe-inline', an injected inline <script> or onerror handler is refused even if the HTML injection exists — damage control, not a replacement for escaping.

followUps.question: Do ORMs make SQL injection impossible?
followUps.answer: They parameterise normal queries, but raw-query helpers with string concatenation (e.g. building a WHERE clause or ORDER BY from input) are still injectable. Use the placeholder APIs and allowlist identifiers.

questions.title: How should you store passwords? (hashing, salting, bcrypt/Argon2 — why not SHA-256)
questions.prompt: How should a backend store user passwords? Explain **hashing vs encryption**, what a **salt** is and what it defends against, why a fast hash like **SHA-256** is the wrong tool, and how **bcrypt**, **scrypt** or **Argon2id** fix it. How does login verification work if the salt is random?
hints: If the database leaks, the attacker has every hash and unlimited offline time. What limits how many guesses per second they can try?
Two users with the password 'Dhaka@123': without a salt their hashes are identical. Why is that bad?
bcrypt stores the algorithm, cost and salt inside the hash string, so verification re-hashes the attempt with the same salt and cost and compares.

approaches.name: Weak answer
approaches.idea: "Hash it with SHA-256 (or MD5) so it's secure" — or encrypt passwords so admins can recover them.

approaches.name: Strong answer
approaches.idea: One-way, slow, salted hashing with a tunable work factor (Argon2id / scrypt / bcrypt / PBKDF2), salts vs rainbow tables, speed vs GPU cracking with numbers, the self-describing hash string, constant-time comparison, rehash on login, optional pepper, plus rate limiting and MFA.

solution.summary: Passwords must be stored with a slow, salted, one-way password-hashing function — Argon2id, scrypt or bcrypt — never as plain text, never encrypted, and never with a fast hash like SHA-256. A unique random salt per user makes identical passwords hash differently and defeats precomputed rainbow tables, while the tunable work factor makes each guess cost hundreds of milliseconds instead of microseconds, so a leaked database can't be brute-forced at GPU speed. At login you re-hash the attempt with the salt and cost stored in the hash string and compare in constant time.
solution.explanation:
**Hashing, not encryption**
Encryption is reversible with a key — if the key leaks (and it lives on the same servers), every password leaks. A **hash** is one-way: you can only check a guess by hashing it and comparing. Nobody, including admins, should be able to recover a password; "forgot password" means *reset*, never *send*.

**Why a salt**
Without a salt, `SHA-256("Dhaka@123")` is the same for every user on every site:
- attackers use **rainbow tables** / precomputed hashes of billions of common passwords;
- identical hashes in your table reveal which users share a password.

A **salt** is a random value (16 bytes) generated **per user**, stored next to the hash and mixed into it. Every hash becomes unique, precomputation is useless, and the attacker must attack each user separately.

**Why salted SHA-256 is still wrong**
SHA-256 is designed to be **fast** — a single modern GPU computes billions of SHA-256 hashes per second, so most human-chosen passwords in a leaked salted-SHA-256 table fall quickly. Password-hashing functions are **deliberately slow and tunable**:
- **Argon2id** — winner of the Password Hashing Competition and OWASP's first choice; **memory-hard** (each guess needs e.g. 19–64 MiB of RAM), which cripples GPU/ASIC parallelism.
- **scrypt** — also memory-hard (OWASP suggests N=2^17, r=8, p=1).
- **bcrypt** — CPU-hard with cost factor `2^cost` rounds; uses only the first **72 bytes** of the password.
- **PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256** with ~600,000 iterations — when FIPS compliance is required.

Measured on a laptop with `bcryptjs` (the pure-JavaScript bcrypt used in this project): cost 10 ≈ 96 ms, 11 ≈ 174 ms, 12 ≈ 329 ms — each +1 doubles the work — while one SHA-256 of a short string takes about 2 µs in Node. That is roughly **150,000× slower per guess** in this test (on GPUs the gap is far larger, because SHA-256 parallelises extremely well), yet an invisible delay for one legitimate login.

**The bcrypt string is self-describing**
`$2b$12$` + 22 characters of **salt** + 31 characters of **hash** (60 characters total): algorithm version `2b`, cost `12`, salt, hash. Verification needs no separate salt column: `bcrypt.compare(attempt, stored)` reads the salt and cost from the string, re-hashes the attempt and compares in constant time.

**Operational must-dos**
- Rehash on a successful login when you raise the cost or migrate algorithms (check `bcrypt.getRounds(hash)`).
- Optional **pepper**: a secret key kept outside the database (secret manager/HSM) and mixed in, so a database-only leak isn't enough.
- Hash asynchronously so logins don't block the event loop; rate-limit login; same error for unknown email and wrong password; offer MFA; reject known-breached passwords.
- In Spring Boot use `BCryptPasswordEncoder` or `Argon2PasswordEncoder`; in Node, `bcrypt`/`bcryptjs` or `argon2` (recent Node 24 releases also ship an experimental `crypto.argon2`).

code.code:
import hashlib
import hmac
import os

N, R, P = 2**17, 8, 1  # scrypt cost (OWASP minimum): CPU- and memory-hard, ~128 MiB per hash
MAXMEM = 256 * 1024 * 1024


def hash_password(password):
    salt = os.urandom(16)  # unique per user
    digest = hashlib.scrypt(password.encode(), salt=salt, n=N, r=R, p=P, maxmem=MAXMEM, dklen=32)
    return f"scrypt${N}${R}${P}${salt.hex()}${digest.hex()}"


def verify_password(attempt, stored):
    _, n, r, p, salt_hex, digest_hex = stored.split("$")
    digest = hashlib.scrypt(attempt.encode(), salt=bytes.fromhex(salt_hex),
                            n=int(n), r=int(r), p=int(p), maxmem=MAXMEM, dklen=32)
    return hmac.compare_digest(digest.hex(), digest_hex)  # constant-time


alice = hash_password("Dhaka@123")
bob = hash_password("Dhaka@123")
print(alice == bob)  # False: different salts
print(verify_password("Dhaka@123", alice), verify_password("dhaka@123", alice))  # True False

keyPoints: Hash (one-way), never encrypt or store plain passwords
Unique random salt per user defeats rainbow tables and hides shared passwords
Use slow, tunable KDFs: Argon2id (memory-hard), scrypt, bcrypt, PBKDF2 — never fast SHA-256
bcrypt string embeds version, cost and salt; compare in constant time
Rehash when raising cost; rate-limit logins; generic errors; MFA

followUps.question: What is a pepper?
followUps.answer: A secret value (stored in a secret manager or HSM, not in the database) mixed into every password hash, typically via HMAC. If only the database leaks, the attacker cannot even start guessing; if the pepper leaks too, you are back to the salted-hash protection.

followUps.question: How do you migrate old SHA-1 hashes to bcrypt without forcing resets?
followUps.answer: Wrap them: store bcrypt(sha1_hash) for every user immediately, mark the scheme, and verify with bcrypt(sha1(attempt)). On each successful login, rehash the plain password directly with bcrypt (or Argon2id) and update the scheme.

questions.title: HTTP caching: Cache-Control, ETag and 304 Not Modified
questions.prompt: Explain how browsers and CDNs cache HTTP responses. What do the **`Cache-Control`** directives `max-age`, `no-cache`, `no-store`, `private`, `public`, `immutable` and `s-maxage` mean? How do **`ETag`** / `If-None-Match` and **`304 Not Modified`** work, and what policy would you give HTML pages, hashed JS/CSS bundles and a user's private API data?
hints: Two separate questions: is the stored copy still fresh (no request at all)? If not, has it changed (ask the server cheaply)?
no-cache does not mean 'don't cache' — it means 'always revalidate before using'.
A file name containing a content hash can never change, so it can be cached for a year; the HTML that references it must be revalidated.

approaches.name: Weak answer
approaches.idea: "Set Cache-Control: no-cache to disable caching." Misreads the directive and cannot explain ETags.

approaches.name: Strong answer
approaches.idea: Separates freshness (max-age, s-maxage) from validation (ETag/Last-Modified → 304), explains each directive and private vs shared caches, and gives a concrete per-resource policy with cache busting through hashed file names.

solution.summary: Caching has two layers. Freshness: Cache-Control: max-age=N lets the browser or CDN reuse a response for N seconds without contacting the server at all. Validation: once the copy is stale, the client sends its stored ETag in If-None-Match and the server answers 304 Not Modified with no body if nothing changed. In practice: hashed static assets get max-age=31536000, immutable; HTML gets no-cache so it always revalidates; personal data gets private, no-cache — and truly sensitive data no-store.
solution.explanation:
**1. Freshness — skip the request entirely**
`Cache-Control: max-age=60` → for 60 seconds the browser (and shared caches) serve the stored copy with **zero network traffic**. After that the copy is **stale**.
- `s-maxage=300` — overrides `max-age` for **shared** caches (CDNs, proxies).
- `public` — any cache may store it; `private` — only the user's browser (never a CDN) — for personalised responses.
- `immutable` — the content will never change while fresh, so don't even revalidate on reload.
- `stale-while-revalidate=60` — serve the stale copy for up to 60 s while refreshing it in the background.

**2. Validation — ask cheaply whether it changed**
- The server sends a validator: **`ETag: W/"32-SctKcc…"`** (a fingerprint of the content; `W/` = weak) and/or `Last-Modified`.
- When the copy is stale the browser sends **`If-None-Match: W/"32-SctKcc…"`** (or `If-Modified-Since`).
- Unchanged → **`304 Not Modified`** with headers only, no body — saves bandwidth (the server may still do the work to compute the ETag). Changed → `200` with the new body and a new ETag.
- Express generates weak ETags for `res.send`/`res.json` automatically and answers 304 when the request's validator matches.

**3. Directives people mix up**
- **`no-cache`** — you *may store* it, but must **revalidate before every use** (cheap with ETag → 304).
- **`no-store`** — **never store** it anywhere: bank statements, OTP pages, personal documents.
- `must-revalidate` — once stale, never use it without successful revalidation (not even offline).
- `Expires` and `Pragma: no-cache` — HTTP/1.0 leftovers; `Cache-Control` wins.

**4. A practical policy**

| Resource | Cache-Control | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `app.3f9a1c.js`, `styles.8b2e.css`, fonts, hashed images | `public, max-age=31536000, immutable` | the file name changes when the content changes (cache busting) |
| HTML pages | `no-cache` (+ ETag) | always pick up a new deploy; a cheap 304 when unchanged |
| Public API data (product list) | `public, max-age=60, s-maxage=300, stale-while-revalidate=60` | slightly stale is fine; the CDN absorbs traffic |
| User-specific API data | `private, no-cache` | browser only, always revalidated |
| Sensitive data | `no-store` | must never be written to a cache |

Also send `Vary: Accept-Encoding` (and `Vary: Origin` with CORS) so caches keep separate copies of each variant.
keyPoints: Freshness (max-age) avoids the request; validation (ETag → 304) avoids the body
no-cache = store but revalidate; no-store = never store
private = browser only; public/s-maxage for CDNs
Hashed assets: max-age=31536000, immutable; HTML: no-cache
Vary on headers that change the response (Accept-Encoding, Origin)

steps.note: First visit: `200` with the body, `Cache-Control: public, max-age=60` and an `ETag` that Express computed from the body. The browser stores all of it.
At 30 s the copy is **fresh** (age 30 < 60): it is used directly — **no network request at all**.
At 70 s the copy is **stale**. The browser revalidates with `If-None-Match`; nothing changed, so Express answers **`304 Not Modified`** with an empty body and the copy is fresh again.
At 100 s the price changes on the server, but the browser copy is still fresh (age 30) and shows the **old price 4500**. That is the trade-off of `max-age`: up to 60 s of staleness.
At 140 s the copy is stale again; the ETag no longer matches, so the server sends **`200` with the new body and a new ETag**.
At 150 s the new copy is fresh — served locally with the new price. Two real requests in 150 s, one of them body-less.

followUps.question: Strong vs weak ETag?
followUps.answer: A strong ETag ("abc") promises byte-for-byte identical content; a weak one (W/"abc") promises semantically equivalent content (e.g. same JSON regardless of compression). Weak ETags are fine for If-None-Match revalidation; range requests need strong ones.

followUps.question: How do you force users onto a new JavaScript bundle after a deploy?
followUps.answer: Content-hash the file names (app.3f9a1c.js) so every change creates a new URL, cache those for a year as immutable, and serve the HTML with no-cache so it always references the latest bundle names.

questions.title: REST vs GraphQL vs gRPC — when would you use each?
questions.prompt: Compare **REST**, **GraphQL** and **gRPC**: data format, transport, how clients ask for data, caching, tooling and typical use cases. A mobile app's home screen needs a user, their last 3 orders and each order's items — how would each style fetch that?
hints: Count the round trips and the unused fields each style returns for the home-screen example.
GraphQL: one endpoint, the client describes the response shape. gRPC: contract-first .proto, binary Protobuf over HTTP/2.
Think about who the client is: a third-party developer, a bandwidth-limited mobile app, or another internal microservice.

approaches.name: Weak answer
approaches.idea: "GraphQL is the new REST, gRPC is faster." No trade-offs, no use cases.

approaches.name: Strong answer
approaches.idea: Contrasts resource-oriented REST (HTTP semantics, caching, simplicity; over/under-fetching), GraphQL (typed schema, client-shaped queries, one round trip; caching, N+1 resolvers, query limits), gRPC (Protobuf contracts, HTTP/2 streaming, codegen; browsers need gRPC-Web) and maps each to a client type.

solution.summary: REST exposes resources at URLs and uses HTTP methods, status codes and caching — simple and universal, but clients often over- or under-fetch and need several round trips. GraphQL exposes one typed endpoint where the client asks for exactly the fields it needs in a single query — great for complex UIs and mobile apps, at the cost of harder caching and resolver performance work. gRPC uses Protobuf contracts and binary messages over HTTP/2 with streaming and generated clients — the fastest option for internal service-to-service calls, but not callable directly from browsers.
solution.explanation:
**REST**
- Resources (`/users/42`, `/users/42/orders`) + HTTP methods, usually JSON.
- Uses HTTP fully: status codes, **HTTP caching** (ETags, CDNs), idempotent retries, easy debugging with curl.
- Weaknesses: **over-fetching** (the user endpoint returns 30 fields, the screen needs 2) and **under-fetching** (user, then orders, then items per order → several round trips, painful on mobile networks). Teams often add a backend-for-frontend endpoint per screen.

**GraphQL**
- One endpoint (`POST /graphql`), a **typed schema**, and queries that describe the exact response shape → one round trip, no unused fields.
- Strong tooling: introspection, autocomplete, generated TypeScript types; the schema evolves by adding fields and deprecating old ones, usually without versions.
- Costs: HTTP caching is harder (POST to one URL → client caches such as Apollo/Relay, persisted queries), the **N+1 problem** in resolvers (batch with **DataLoader**), and you must limit **query depth and complexity** so a client can't request an enormous nested tree. Errors often come back as HTTP 200 with an `errors` array.

**gRPC**
- **Contract-first**: services and messages in a `.proto` file, with generated clients and servers for Go, Java, Node, Python…
- **Protobuf** binary encoding (smaller and faster to parse than JSON) over **HTTP/2** (multiplexing, header compression).
- Four call types: unary, server streaming, client streaming and **bidirectional streaming**; deadlines and cancellation built in.
- Popular between internal microservices (e.g. order service ↔ payment service).
- Browsers can't make raw gRPC calls → **gRPC-Web** plus a proxy (e.g. Envoy); binary payloads are harder to inspect by hand.

**Choosing**
- Public or partner API, simple CRUD, cache-heavy → **REST**.
- Rich frontend or mobile app aggregating many entities, many client teams → **GraphQL** (often a gateway in front of REST/gRPC services).
- Internal service-to-service, low latency, streaming, polyglot teams → **gRPC**.

Real systems mix them: REST for the public API, GraphQL for the apps, gRPC between services.
keyPoints: REST: resources + HTTP semantics, great caching, risk of over/under-fetching
GraphQL: one typed endpoint, client picks fields, one round trip; harder caching, N+1 → DataLoader, limit query cost
gRPC: Protobuf over HTTP/2, codegen, streaming, fast; browsers need gRPC-Web
Public APIs → REST; rich UIs/mobile → GraphQL; internal services → gRPC
Real systems mix them

followUps.question: What is the N+1 problem in GraphQL and how is it solved?

followUps.question: Why is gRPC faster than JSON REST?

questions.title: WebSockets vs polling vs Server-Sent Events (real-time updates)
questions.prompt: A food-delivery app must show **live order status**, and its support page needs **two-way chat**. Compare **short polling**, **long polling**, **Server-Sent Events (SSE)** and **WebSockets**: how each works, latency, server cost and direction of data — and pick one for each feature.
hints: Who starts each message, and how many HTTP requests does each technique need per update?
SSE is one long-lived HTTP response the server keeps writing to; a WebSocket upgrades the connection to a full-duplex protocol.
One-way server→client updates fit SSE; frequent messages in both directions fit WebSockets.

approaches.name: Weak answer
approaches.idea: "Use WebSockets for everything real-time." Ignores simpler options and the cost of stateful connections.

approaches.name: Strong answer
approaches.idea: Explains each mechanism with latency/overhead trade-offs, the 101 upgrade handshake, SSE auto-reconnect with Last-Event-ID, scaling concerns (connection counts, pub/sub between servers) and chooses per feature.

solution.summary: Short polling asks the server every few seconds — simple but wasteful and laggy. Long polling holds each request open until there is news, then the client immediately asks again. Server-Sent Events keep one HTTP response open and stream text events from server to client with automatic reconnection — ideal for notifications, live order status and streaming LLM tokens. WebSockets upgrade the connection to a persistent full-duplex channel for frequent two-way messages such as chat or multiplayer games, at the cost of stateful connections you must scale and manage yourself.
solution.explanation:
**Short polling** — `setInterval(() => fetch('/api/orders/42/status'), 5000)`.
- Simple, works everywhere, stateless servers.
- Latency up to the interval; most responses say "no change" → wasted requests, battery and server load.

**Long polling** — the client sends a request; the server **holds** it until there is an update (or ~30 s pass), responds, and the client immediately sends the next request.
- Near real-time over plain HTTP, works through any proxy.
- A full HTTP request (headers, auth) per message; many held connections; message ordering needs care.

**Server-Sent Events (SSE)**
- Client: `new EventSource('/api/orders/42/events')`. The server answers `Content-Type: text/event-stream` and keeps writing blocks like `id: 3`, `event: status`, `data: {...}` followed by a blank line.
- **One-way, server → client**, UTF-8 text only.
- Built-in **automatic reconnection**; the browser sends `Last-Event-ID` so the server can resume missed events; `retry:` sets the delay.
- Plain HTTP → works with existing cookies/auth, proxies and HTTP/2 multiplexing. Over HTTP/1.1 browsers allow only about 6 connections per host, so many tabs can exhaust them (not an issue with HTTP/2).
- Great for: order/delivery status, notifications, live scores, dashboards, streaming AI responses token by token.

**WebSockets**
- Starts as HTTP: `GET /chat` with `Upgrade: websocket` and `Sec-WebSocket-Key` → the server replies **`101 Switching Protocols`** → the TCP connection becomes a **full-duplex** message channel (`ws://`, or `wss://` over TLS).
- Tiny per-message framing overhead, text **and binary** frames, either side can send at any time.
- You implement heartbeats, reconnection with backoff and message acknowledgements yourself (or use a library such as Socket.IO). The server sends ping frames and browsers answer pong automatically; the browser API can't send pings, so clients use app-level heartbeat messages.
- Scaling: connections are **long-lived and stateful** → the load balancer must support them, and a pub/sub backbone (Redis, NATS) delivers messages to users connected to *other* servers; plan capacity for open connections.
- Great for: chat, multiplayer games, collaborative editing, trading screens.

**For the example**: live order status → **SSE** (server → client only, simple, auto-reconnect); support chat → **WebSocket**; an admin page refreshed every minute → plain **polling** is fine.
keyPoints: Short polling: simple, wasteful, latency up to the interval
Long polling: near real-time over plain HTTP, one request per message
SSE: one HTTP response, server→client text events, auto-reconnect + Last-Event-ID
WebSocket: 101 upgrade → full-duplex, binary/text, you handle heartbeats and reconnects
Scale stateful connections with pub/sub (Redis) and load balancers that support them

followUps.question: How do you scale WebSockets across several servers?
followUps.answer: Each server keeps its own connections; publish every message to a shared bus (Redis pub/sub, NATS, Kafka) that all servers subscribe to, and each delivers it to its local sockets. The load balancer must support long-lived upgraded connections (sticky sessions help with fallbacks).

followUps.question: How do LLM chat apps stream answers token by token?
followUps.answer: Usually with SSE (or a streamed fetch response): the request is a normal POST, and the server writes tokens as data: events while generating, so the UI renders text progressively without WebSocket infrastructure.

questions.title: How does the browser render a page? (critical rendering path)
questions.prompt: After the HTML arrives, how does the browser turn it into pixels? Explain the **critical rendering path** — DOM, CSSOM, render tree, layout, paint, composite — why CSS and some JavaScript are **render-blocking**, the difference between plain `<script>`, `async` and `defer`, and how you'd speed up the first render.
hints: The browser needs both the DOM and the CSSOM before it can paint anything styled.
A classic script stops the HTML parser until it downloads and runs. What do async and defer change?
Changing width or top forces layout; changing transform or opacity can skip straight to compositing.

approaches.name: Weak answer
approaches.idea: "The browser reads the HTML and shows it; put scripts at the bottom." No mechanism, no async/defer, no metrics.

approaches.name: Strong answer
approaches.idea: Walks through parse → DOM, CSS → CSSOM, render tree, layout, paint, composite; explains render-blocking CSS and parser-blocking JS, async vs defer vs module, reflow vs repaint and layout thrashing, and optimisations tied to Core Web Vitals (LCP, INP, CLS).

solution.summary: The browser parses HTML into the DOM and CSS into the CSSOM, combines them into a render tree of visible elements, computes each element's geometry (layout), fills in pixels (paint) and composites the layers on the GPU. CSS is render-blocking and classic scripts block the HTML parser, so for a fast first render you keep critical CSS small (or inline it), load scripts with defer or async, prioritise the hero image and preload fonts, and avoid layout-thrashing JavaScript.
solution.explanation: **The steps** 1. **Parse HTML → DOM** (bytes → tokens → nodes → tree), incrementally as bytes arrive. A **preload scanner** looks ahead and starts downloading images, CSS and scripts early. 2. **Parse CSS → CSSOM**. CSS is **render-blocking**: the browser won't paint until the stylesheets in `` are loaded (otherwise you'd see a flash of unstyled content). 3. **Render tree** = DOM + CSSOM, visible nodes only (`display: none` elements and `` are left out; `visibility: hidden` elements stay because they take up space). 4. **Layout (reflow)** — compute every box's size and position for the current viewport. 5. **Paint** — fill in pixels (text, colours, borders, shadows, images) into layers. 6. **Composite** — the GPU combines the layers in order. Changes to `transform` and `opacity` can often be done in this step alone, which is why they animate smoothly. **JavaScript and the parser** - `
keyPoints: HTML → DOM, CSS → CSSOM → render tree → layout → paint → composite
CSS is render-blocking; classic scripts are parser-blocking
defer: run after parsing, in order; async: run on arrival, any order; modules are deferred
Geometry changes cost layout; transform/opacity can be composite-only
Optimise for LCP, INP and CLS: small critical CSS, defer JS, prioritise the hero image, reserve image space

steps.note: **Classic `<script src>`** in `<head>`: the parser stops while the script downloads (40 ms) and runs (10 ms); the rest of the document waits.
**`async`**: downloads in parallel and runs **as soon as it arrives**, pausing the parser only for execution. Order between async scripts is not guaranteed.
**`defer`**: downloads in parallel and runs **after parsing finishes**, in document order, just before `DOMContentLoaded`. The parser is never blocked.
**CSS is render-blocking**: the DOM is ready at 30 ms, but nothing is painted until app.css arrives and the CSSOM is built — first paint at ~60 ms. Keep critical CSS small.

followUps.question: What are LCP, INP and CLS?
followUps.answer: Core Web Vitals: Largest Contentful Paint (when the main content is visible; good ≤ 2.5 s), Interaction to Next Paint (responsiveness to input; good ≤ 200 ms; replaced FID in March 2024) and Cumulative Layout Shift (visual stability; good ≤ 0.1).

followUps.question: What is the difference between DOMContentLoaded and load?
followUps.answer: DOMContentLoaded fires when the HTML is parsed and deferred scripts have run; load fires later, when all dependent resources such as images, stylesheets and iframes have finished loading.

quiz.question: Which HTTP method is idempotent but NOT safe?
quiz.explanation: PUT changes state (not safe) but repeating it leaves the same state (idempotent). GET and OPTIONS are safe; POST is neither.

quiz.question: A logged-in normal user calls an admin-only endpoint. Which status code fits best?
quiz.explanation: The user is authenticated but not permitted → 403. 401 means missing or invalid credentials; logging in again would not help here.

quiz.question: Which redirect is permanent AND guarantees the method and body are reused?
quiz.explanation: 308 = permanent + same method; 307 = temporary + same method. 301/302 historically let browsers change POST to GET.

quiz.question: What does Cache-Control: no-cache mean?
options: The response must never be stored
It may be stored but must be revalidated before every use
Cache it for 0 seconds, then delete it
quiz.explanation: no-cache allows storing but requires revalidation (cheap with ETag → 304). "Never store" is no-store.

quiz.question: A page on https://app.example.com sends fetch PUT with a JSON body to https://api.example.com. What happens first?
options: The browser sends an OPTIONS preflight
The browser blocks it because the subdomains differ
The server sends a CORS challenge
quiz.explanation: Different subdomain = different origin, and PUT + application/json make it non-simple, so the browser asks with OPTIONS first.

quiz.question: The client uses fetch(url, { credentials: 'include' }). Which response header value makes the browser reject the response?
quiz.explanation: With credentials the server must name the exact origin; the wildcard * is not allowed.

quiz.question: Which cookie attribute stops JavaScript from reading the cookie?
quiz.explanation: HttpOnly hides the cookie from document.cookie, so an XSS script cannot read it. Secure limits it to HTTPS; SameSite limits cross-site sending.

quiz.question: Where is sessionStorage data visible?
options: Only in the tab that created it, until that tab closes
In all tabs of the same origin
On the server with every request
In all origins of the browser
quiz.explanation: sessionStorage is per tab (and origin) and cleared when the tab closes; localStorage is shared by all tabs of the origin. Neither is sent to the server.

quiz.question: In the OAuth 2.0 code flow with PKCE, what does the client put in the initial /authorize redirect?
quiz.explanation: Only the hash travels through the browser. The verifier is sent later on the back-channel token request, so an intercepted code is useless.

quiz.question: Why is SHA-256 a poor choice for storing passwords, even with a salt?
options: It is too fast — attackers can test billions of guesses per second
It can be decrypted with the server key
quiz.explanation: Salts stop precomputed tables, but a GPU can still test billions of salted SHA-256 guesses per second. Argon2id, scrypt and bcrypt are deliberately slow and tunable.

quiz.question: What does this print?
options: SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = '' OR '1'='1'
SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = '\' OR \'1\'=\'1'
SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = ''' OR ''1''=''1'
quiz.explanation: String concatenation pastes the input into the SQL text: the quote closes the string and OR '1'='1' is always true — classic SQL injection. Use a parameterised query instead.

quiz.question: Which technique gives one-way server→client streaming over plain HTTP with automatic reconnection?
quiz.explanation: SSE keeps one text/event-stream response open, and EventSource reconnects automatically sending Last-Event-ID. WebSockets are full duplex but reconnection is up to you.
